property_summary: For every caller, the reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (_owner) (which equals the deployer after initialize), whereas the mutant returns address(0) and thus can differ for some callers/inputs.

For any caller the reference contract returns the stored owner address (independent of msg.sender); the mutant returns msg.sender instead, so there exists a caller for which owner() differs from the stored owner.

For every deployment/initializer call, the contract's owner() returns the stored owner address (the deployer after initialize); the mutant that always returns address(this) violates this because for many deployed instances address(this) != stored owner.

For any caller who is the current owner and any non-zero newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() must equal the provided newOwner; the mutant that sets owner to address(0) violates this rule for some inputs.

For any nonzero newOwner address, transferOwnership called by the current owner succeeds on the reference; the mutant allows setting the zero address as owner (breaking the invariant that owner is never zero after transferOwnership by owner).

After a transferOwnership call made by the current owner, the reference contract never sets owner to the zero address (owner() != address(0)) for any newOwner; the mutant allows owner() == address(0) when newOwner == address(0), violating this invariant.

For any caller address X and any newOwner Y, the correct contract allows transferOwnership only when the caller is the current owner and after the call owner() == Y; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check so non-owners can call transferOwnership and thus for some (caller, newOwner) combinations the post-call owner differs between reference and mutant.

For all callers addr and target newOwner, only the current owner may successfully call transferOwnership and after a successful call owner() == newOwner; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check allowing non-owners to call transferOwnership, so there exist caller/newOwner pairs where owner() differs between reference and mutant.

For every nonzero address input, calling updateRoundImplementation(...) on the correct contract always sets roundImplementation to the provided address and returns (does not allow zero), whereas the mutant allows setting it to address(0) — so the property: if newRoundImplementation != address(0) then after the call roundImplementation == newRoundImplementation (holds for reference for all inputs) but the mutant can violate the intended prohibition by accepting address(0).

For every input address newImpl, calling updateRoundImplementation(newImpl) on the correct contract either (a) reverts if caller not owner or (b) sets roundImplementation to newImpl when caller is owner and newImpl != address(0); the mutant violates the invariant that the owner cannot set roundImplementation to address(0) by allowing address(0) to be stored — so the reference never results in roundImplementation == address(0) after an owner call with newImpl == address(0) (it reverts), while the mutant does set it to address(0).

For any caller who is the owner, calling updateRoundImplementation(newRoundImplementation) never results in roundImplementation being address(0) (the reference reverts on a zero newRoundImplementation), while the mutant allows the owner to set roundImplementation to address(0).

For any caller (fuzzed as operatorAddr) that is the owner, calling updateRoundImplementation(newImpl) will always revert if newImpl == address(0) on the reference (so roundImplementation never becomes address(0)); the mutant allows the call to succeed and sets roundImplementation to address(0), so the property is violated for some fuzz input where owner calls with newImpl == address(0).

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling updateRoundImplementation(newImpl) never results in c.roundImplementation() being address(0) after the call (the reference rejects a zero newImpl, but the mutant accepts and stores address(0)).

For any non-zero address input, the reference contract allows the owner to set roundImplementation to that non-zero address (so c.roundImplementation() equals the provided address after the call), whereas the mutant wrongly only permits setting it to address(0), so for some non-zero address inputs the mutant's stored roundImplementation differs from the input (and from the reference).

For every caller address, when the current owner (initial owner after initialize) calls updateRoundImplementation with a non-zero address, the reference contract will successfully set roundImplementation to that address; the mutant (which requires owner() == address(0)) prevents the real owner from succeeding and thus for some fuzzed caller/address inputs the stored roundImplementation differs.

For any caller who is the owner and any address input, calling updateAlloSettings(newAddr) updates c.alloSettings() to equal newAddr; the mutant emits an event but does not update the state, so for some newAddr the post-call getter will differ.

For any caller that is the contract owner and any input address, calling updateAlloSettings(newAlloSettings) sets c.alloSettings() equal to the provided newAlloSettings; the mutant instead always sets alloSettings to the zero address, breaking this property for inputs where newAlloSettings != address(0).

For any caller, calling updateAlloSettings(newAddr) by the contract owner (owner() == msg.sender) always sets c.alloSettings() to newAddr; the mutant that checks owner() == address(0) instead can allow the call to revert or prevent owner from updating, so there exist inputs (an owner caller and some newAddr) where reference updates alloSettings but mutant does not.
